problems.title: A normalized minimum does not encode the raw obstacle threshold
problems.source_location: Section 3.1.3, Calculation of Affordance Map and Eq.(3), PDF p.7; Section 4.1 threshold, p.7
claim: For threshold-admissible navigable points the obstacle preference is min–max normalized, but Eq.(3) uses its zero value as the final exclusion mask. Target-distance normalization also divides by its range without a stated tie rule.
analysis: Let the already processed obstacle cloud be \(O=\{(0,0)\}\), target \(T=(1,0)\), candidates \(n_1=(1/2,0)\), \(n_2=(3/4,0)\), and threshold \(\tau_o=1/4\). Both are safe under the stated raw-distance threshold. Their obstacle distances are \((1/2,3/4)\), hence normalized preferences \((0,1)\); their inverse target preferences are \((0,1)\). Eq.(3) returns \((0,1)\), whereas a raw-distance mask followed by the stated clipping returns \((0.1,1)\). Every safe minimum is similarly excluded when \(d_{\max}>d_{\min}\ge\tau_o\).

Valid geometry also gives undefined ranges. Candidates \((\pm1/2,0)\) around the same obstacle have constant safe obstacle distance and yield \(0/0\). Alternatively, the original candidates with target \((5/8,0)\) have equal target distances \(1/8\), so semantic normalization yields \(0/0\).
result: The literal formulas need a normalization and tie convention. If excluding safe minima is intentional, it is an additional preference rule; normalization over a larger set containing obstacles could remove the first example. No route or success-rate change is established.
assumptions: Distances are finite, candidates nonempty, and extrema are over the navigable points being scored.
repair: Separate the mask \(s(n)=\mathbf1\{d_o(n)\ge\tau_o\}\) from preference. Let \(q\) be inverse target normalization with an explicit common value when distances tie, and set \(\widehat a_f=s\,\operatorname{clip}(q,0.1,1)\). The positive clipped factor makes zero equivalent to raw threshold exclusion. This restores only that property, not collision-free planning.
